prime.problem: An attention score is a dot product, so it adds up head_size products. Make the head wider and the scores spread wider, and softmax snaps each row to almost one-hot before training has even started.
prime.fits: The self-attention-head card built softmax(q @ kᵀ) and showed that bigger scores give peakier weights. This card adds the one factor the paper's formula has and ours didn't: dividing the scores by √head_size.
prime.goal: Derive why q·k has variance head_size, predict what an unscaled wide head does to softmax, and pick the right divisor (√head_size, not head_size or √C).

attend: Which property of variance makes the spread of q·k grow with head_size rather than stay fixed?
Why a square root: what would dividing by head_size itself do to the scores?
Softmax only cares about gaps between scores. How does scaling every score by 8 change the gaps, and the weights?
Why does a near one-hot row starve the queries and keys of gradient?
What assumption about q and k does the √head_size rule rely on, and does the crux cell's nn.Linear output meet it?

must: q·k sums head_size products → each product has variance 1 when q and k entries are independent with variance 1 → variances of independent terms add → Var(q·k) ≈ head_size (16.00 at 16, 63.10 at 64)
Multiplying by c multiplies variance by c² → multiplying by 1/√head_size divides the variance by head_size → scores are back near variance 1 whatever the head size (1.000 at 16, 0.986 at 64)

Softmax is exponential in score gaps → wide scores make rows near one-hot (×8 → 0.80 peak, ×50 → 0.99995) → nudging a score barely moves the weights (gradient size 1.57 → 0.67 → 0.00018) → an unscaled wide head starts out copying one token and learns slowly
elevated: The divisor must be the head's own width (k.shape[-1]), not the embedding width C → the Colab's final cell used C**-0.5 → at gpt.py sizes the variance would be 64 / 384 = 0.17, so heads start too flat, closer to a plain average
reference: the paper writes it softmax(QKᵀ/√d<sub>k</sub>)V, Vaswani et al. 2017, section 3.2.1
F.scaled_dot_product_attention applies the same 1/√d scale by default
the illustrative scores [0.1, -0.2, 0.3, -0.2, 0.5] from the video

compress.prompt: From memory, write the chain from "q and k have unit-variance entries" to "softmax stays diffuse at init" in 3–5 sentences, or as an arrow chain. Include the one line of arithmetic that gives Var(q·k) = head_size.
checklist: q·k is a sum of head_size products, each with variance 1
independent variances add, so the sum has variance head_size and standard deviation √head_size
multiplying by 1/√head_size divides the variance by head_size, back to about 1
wide scores make softmax near one-hot, and near one-hot rows pass almost no gradient
the divisor is the head's width, not C (the Colab bug)

retrieve.q: Explain in plain words why a dot product of two random 64-long vectors is typically about 8 in size, while their entries are typically about 1.
answer: 64 products, each of typical size 1 and random sign, partly cancel
typical size is the standard deviation, √64 = 8

retrieve.q: Walk through what happens to Karpathy's row [0.1, -0.2, 0.3, -0.2, 0.5] when every score is multiplied by 8, from the gaps to the final weights.
answer: the gap between 0.5 and 0.3 grows from 0.2 to 1.6, a weight ratio of about e<sup>1.6</sup> ≈ 5
the top weight rises from 0.2872 to 0.8000; the −0.2 entries fall to 0.0030
the row is now close to one-hot, so the token mostly copies one other token

retrieve.q: A colleague proposes dividing scores by head_size instead of √head_size, "to be safe". What does that cost at head_size 64?
answer: scores cluster near 0, so every row starts close to a plain average
the head has to grow its weights a lot before it can attend to anything specific

retrieve.q: Why does the √head_size factor not guarantee unit-variance scores in the crux cell, where q and k come from untrained nn.Linear layers?
answer: the rule assumes q and k entries have variance 1
default nn.Linear outputs had variance about 0.34 and 0.32 there
raw scores had variance 1.92, so scaling brought them to 0.12, flatter than 1

compare.q: Kaiming init scales weights by about 1/√fan_in; attention scales scores by 1/√head_size. What is the shared argument, what is being kept at variance 1 in each case, and how does each fail if you drop the factor?
answer: shared: a sum of n independent terms has variance n times one term's, so divide by √n
Kaiming keeps each layer's activations near unit variance; attention keeps the scores entering softmax near unit variance
without Kaiming, activations grow or shrink layer by layer (tanh saturates); without the attention scale, softmax saturates to one-hot
both are fixes for the starting point only; training can move away from them

compare.q: Both cards shrink numbers that feed a softmax at initialization. What is different about where the softmax sits and what goes wrong in each case?
answer: squash-the-logits: the output softmax over 27 characters; big logits make confident wrong guesses and a high initial loss
scaled attention: a softmax inside the model over earlier tokens; big scores make each token copy one other token
both fail through saturation: near one-hot outputs with tiny gradients

predict.q: The next card uses 4 heads of 8 dims each, with C = 32. If you kept the Colab's bug and scaled by C**-0.5 instead of head_size**-0.5, what would the variance of unit-variance scores be, and would the heads start sharper or flatter than intended?
predict.answer: Flatter. Unscaled variance is head_size = 8; dividing by C = 32 gives 8 / 32 = 0.25 instead of 1, so the typical score is half the intended size (√0.25 = 0.5). The fix, k.shape[-1]**-0.5, divides by 8 and gives 1. With one 32-wide head the bug is invisible, because then C = head_size.

apply.task: In labs/scaled-attention.py, add 256 to the for hs in [16, 64] list and predict both variances before running. Then add a check: with seed 0, draw q and k as torch.randn(1000, 8, 64), form s = q @ k.transpose(-2, -1), and print the mean of the top softmax weight per row, unscaled and scaled by 64**-0.5.
apply.done: You see head_size 256: var(q.k) = 259.85 var(q.k / sqrt(256)) = 1.015, and a mean top weight of about 0.874 unscaled vs 0.360 scaled (a plain average over 8 keys would be 0.125).
apply.hint: Adding 256 at the end of the list keeps the 16 and 64 lines unchanged, because they draw their random numbers first. Reset the seed before the second check.
